newsitem.title: SPAIN: NATO signs new security pact with Ukraine.
newsitem.headline: NATO signs new security pact with Ukraine.

text.p: Ukraine signed a special charter with NATO on Wednesday that will give the former Soviet republic the right to call for "consultations" with NATO if it faces any outside threat.
Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma signed the pact, the "Charter on a Distinctive Partnership between NATO and Ukraine", at the start of the second day of a two-day meeting of NATO leaders in Madrid.

"Madrid 1997 will undoubtably go down in history as a city where the dividing line left by the Cold War in the centre of Europe was eliminated," Kuchma said before signing the charter with 16 NATO heads of state and government.

Ukraine is not seeking to join NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organisation), which on Tuesday extended an invitation of membership to three former Warsaw Pact nations. But the pact marked the culmination of long negotiations on how to strengthen ties without arousing Russian ire.
The Ukrainian leader went out of his way to praise a cooperation treaty signed in May between NATO and Russia as a counterweight to the eastward expansion of the alliance.

"This charter reflects and reinforces the way this continent has changed," U.S. President Bill Clinton told the gathering. "It is natural for Ukraine to reach out to NATO and for NATO to do the same, helping to secure Ukraine formally in the heart of a new undivided, democratic Europe.
"May the charter we sign today be just the opening page in a long history of unity, partnership and peace," Clinton said.

The charter sets up a series of mechanisms for contacts between NATO and Ukraine. There will be an exchange of military missions, with NATO establishing an office in Kiev, and meetings at ambassadorial level will be held once a month.
A NATO-Ukraine Commission will meet twice a year and provide the vehicle for "consultations" at times of regional crisis.

Ukraine, the second most populous of the 15 former Soviet republics with 52 million people, became the world's third largest nuclear power after the Soviet Union split up in 1991. But has since removed all nuclear warheads from its SS-19 and SS-24 long-range missiles.

Ukraine, which was ruled from Moscow for more than three centuries, was the first member of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) grouping former Soviet republics to join NATO's Partnership for Peace Programme.
"This historic document is convincing evidence that on the European continent the new security architecture, based on openness and partnership, is being shaped," Kuchma said.
